title: Airport Route Finder: Non-Stop Routes
description: Check historical OpenFlights routes between two IATA airports; confirm current schedules independently.
summary_sentence: Route records are historical, not a live timetable or booking result.
quick_answer: Enter two IATA codes to search historical directional OpenFlights records for a non-stop route or up to eight one-stop connections. The displayed great-circle distance is between the endpoints, not individual legs.
steps_intro: Airline route maps are marketing; a dataset is an answer. Three steps to a checkable verdict:

use_cases.title: Testing a trip idea before booking sites

body.t: Before fighting with booking engines, learn whether your pair is even a non-stop. If it is not, the hub the finder names is usually the connection the airlines will sell you anyway.
A slightly further airport with a non-stop often beats the near one plus a connection. Run both pairs and let the route structure, not the drive, make the decision.
Network questions — which cities are one stop from everywhere, which regions depend on a single hub — start with pair checks like these against a fixed dataset.
Travel arrangers can answer “is there a direct flight?” with a dataset verdict rather than a shrug, and quote the one-stop hub in the same breath.
Try two IATA codes, such as JFK and LAX. A record in the dataset does not establish current service.
If the data contains no non-stop route, the tool looks for up to eight directional one-stop connections. Confirm any itinerary with airlines.

faq: No. OpenFlights route records are historical and may be outdated; confirm current service with airlines.
Why might a real route be missing?

Datasets age: new routes appear, seasonal routes pause, and small carriers are unevenly covered. If a booking engine sells a non-stop the finder lacks, trust the booking engine and treat the dataset as the thing that is out of date.
What does one-stop via a hub mean?
The dataset has a directed route from the first airport to the hub and another from the hub to the destination. It does not establish schedule compatibility or bookability.
No — the tool answers non-stop and one-stop only, which covers the large majority of practical itineraries and keeps the answer honest.
Are the distances road or air?
The tool shows the great-circle distance between the two endpoint airports, not individual connecting legs.
Do alliances matter to the result?

The dataset records operating routes regardless of alliance. In practice one-stop suggestions are most useful when the hub is served by the same alliance you plan to book with — check that at booking time.
Can I use city names instead of IATA codes?
The finder is built around IATA codes (JFK, LHR, CDG). If you do not know a code, the Airport Distance Calculator's search resolves names to airports first.
